ECE 6390 / Digital signals

Pulses & ISI

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how overlapping pulses can give interference-free samples at the intended decision times.

A Nyquist combined pulse response has h(0) = 1 and h(nT) = 0 at nonzero integer symbol offsets. Neighboring pulses may overlap strongly between sampling instants while contributing zero at the ideal samples.

A raised-cosine response controls the trade between spectral rolloff and time-domain ringing. Its total passband occupied width is approximately (1 + α)Rs, with rolloff 0 ≤ α ≤ 1 and symbol rate Rs = 1/T.

The relevant response includes transmitter, channel, and receiver together. A root-raised-cosine transmitter and matched receiver can form a raised-cosine response; timing error or channel distortion can disrupt its zero-ISI sampling property.

Example

At Rs = 1 Mbaud and α = 0.5, the ideal raised-cosine total RF width is 1.5 MHz. This bandwidth statement uses the passband convention.

    Practice

    1. Why can a zero-ISI pulse shape still show interference when the receiver samples halfway between the intended symbol instants?

    The zero crossings are located at specific integer multiples of T.

    The Nyquist zeros guarantee cancellation only at the intended sample times. A timing offset generally samples neighboring pulses away from their zeros, creating intersymbol interference.
